triage.name: Necrotizing enterocolitis
triage.reason: Premature infant with feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and bloody stools; diagnosis supported by abdominal x-ray showing pneumatosis, a classic surgical neonatal emergency.

age.peak: first 2–4 weeks of life, especially 1–3 weeks after birth in premature infants

demographics: Occurs almost exclusively in newborns; the great majority are premature infants
Risk rises with lower birth weight and earlier gestational age
More common in infants who are formula-fed than exclusively breast-milk-fed
Term infants account for a minority of cases, often with a predisposing condition

risk_factors.text: Formula feeding rather than human milk
Antibiotics started in the first days of life
Congenital heart disease with ductal-dependent circulation

comorbidities: Necrotizing enterocolitis is itself the acute illness; chronic comorbidities are those of prematurity
social_history: Born prematurely and cared for in a neonatal intensive care unit
Often receiving enteral feeds through a tube
exposures: Empiric antibiotics in the newborn period

chief_complaints.text: My baby's belly looks swollen and he won't take his feeds
There is blood in my baby's diaper
My baby keeps vomiting and seems very sleepy

hpi.onset: Gradual over hours to a day or two, in a hospitalized premature newborn who had been feeding and growing
hpi.duration: Symptoms usually present for less than 24–48 hours at the time of evaluation
hpi.progression: Starts with feeding intolerance and a full-looking abdomen, then progresses to bilious emesis, bloody stools, increasing distension and lethargy; can worsen rapidly to shock and perforation
hpi.quality: The infant cannot describe pain; parents and nurses notice a tense, distended, tender abdomen and episodes of crying or grimacing
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; the infant looks increasingly unwell
hpi.timing: Continuous once established, with worsening around feeds

associated_symptoms.text: Feeding intolerance with large gastric residuals
Blood in the stool or a bloody diaper
Temperature instability, either low or high
Redness of the abdominal wall over a loop of bowel

pertinent_negatives: Recent antibiotic exposure with profuse diarrhea (as in Clostridioides difficile colitis)
Projectile non-bilious vomiting in a thriving infant (as in pyloric stenosis)
Bilious vomiting in a well-appearing infant with a scaphoid abdomen (as in malrotation with volvulus)
Failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours (as in Hirschsprung disease)
Known congenital heart disease with cyanotic spells

negatives: Weight loss beyond expected newborn transition
argues_against: Chronic poor weight gain over months
Bilious vomiting in a well-appearing infant with a flat abdomen

atypical.how_it_differs: The youngest and smallest premature infants may show only apnea, bradycardia, temperature instability and poor feeding before any abdominal signs appear.
In term infants, necrotizing enterocolitis often follows a predisposing illness such as congenital heart disease, sepsis or a hypoxic event, and abdominal signs may be the first clue.

Infants with severe immunodeficiency or on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics can present with a picture overlapping Clostridioides difficile colitis, with profuse diarrhea and marked systemic toxicity.

general.mild: Premature infant who is feeding poorly and looks uncomfortable; abdomen mildly full but soft
general.moderate: Ill-appearing, irritable or lethargic, tense distended abdomen, grimaces with handling
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, lethargic, mottled, cool extremities, marked abdominal distension with guarding
general.critical: Shock-like, pale or mottled, unresponsive, rigid abdomen, apnea and bradycardia

labs.caveat: Newborns normally have higher white counts than older children; a normal or even low count can occur with overwhelming sepsis and does not exclude the diagnosis.
Falling platelets are a hallmark of progressive disease and often precede perforation; a rapid drop should prompt reassessment.
A left shift with immature forms supports bacterial sepsis and necrotizing enterocolitis.
Anemia from blood loss into the gut and from marrow suppression in sepsis; also reflects the anemia of prematurity.
Hyponatremia from third-spacing of fluid into the bowel wall and peritoneum; a falling sodium is a marker of worsening disease.
Hyperkalemia from tissue breakdown, acidosis and renal hypoperfusion; can be life-threatening.
Metabolic acidosis from bowel ischemia and lactic acid; a low bicarbonate is a key severity marker.
Rises with dehydration and poor renal perfusion.
Newborn creatinine initially reflects maternal values; a rising creatinine suggests acute kidney injury from hypoperfusion.
Hypoglycemia is common in the sick premature infant and must be corrected promptly.
Elevated lactate reflects intestinal ischemia and systemic hypoperfusion; a rising value suggests perforation or shock.
May be normal early; serial values are more useful than a single measurement.
Supports a bacterial cause and systemic infection but is not required for diagnosis.
Prolonged in disseminated intravascular coagulation and in the sick premature infant.
Arterial or capillary blood gas; metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

imaging.study: Abdominal x-ray (supine and left lateral decubitus or cross-table lateral)
imaging.preferred_when: First-line study in any infant with suspected necrotizing enterocolitis

findings.text: Diffusely dilated loops of bowel with a paucity of gas
Pneumatosis intestinalis: intramural gas appearing as bubbly or linear lucencies within the bowel wall
Portal venous gas: branching lucencies over the liver
Fixed, dilated loop of bowel that does not change on serial films
Pneumoperitoneum: free intraperitoneal air indicating perforation
Ascites with a generalized ground-glass appearance and separation of bowel loops
Normal or nonspecific bowel gas pattern early in the disease

imaging.preferred_when: When plain films are equivocal or to assess bowel viability and free fluid

findings.text: Intramural gas (pneumatosis) seen as echogenic foci within the bowel wall
Absent or diminished bowel wall perfusion on Doppler

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Not routinely indicated in neonates; reserved for unusual presentations or when the diagnosis remains unclear after plain films and ultrasound
Pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas
Bowel wall thickening and decreased enhancement
Not indicated for suspected necrotizing enterocolitis; used to evaluate malrotation or obstruction when the presentation is atypical

initial.why: Assesses leukocytosis or leukopenia, left shift, anemia and thrombocytopenia, which track severity
Detects hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia and renal function changes
Marker of intestinal ischemia and systemic hypoperfusion
Supports inflammation and infection; serial values help follow the course
Baseline coagulation studies before surgery and to detect disseminated intravascular coagulation
Assesses acid-base status and oxygenation in the sick infant

initial.test: Abdominal x-ray (supine and left lateral decubitus or cross-table lateral)
initial.why: First-line imaging; looks for pneumatosis, portal venous gas, fixed loops and free air

initial.only_if: suspected sepsis or before starting antibiotics

initial.why: Evaluates for infectious colitis when diarrhea is prominent
initial.only_if: profuse diarrhea or an outbreak setting

supporting.why: Detects pneumatosis, portal venous gas, free fluid and poor bowel perfusion when plain films are equivocal
Supports a bacterial cause and systemic infection
Reserved for atypical presentations or when the diagnosis remains unclear
supporting.only_if: plain films and ultrasound are nondiagnostic and the infant is stable

not_indicated.why: Not routine in neonates; radiation exposure and transport risk outweigh benefit when plain films are diagnostic
not_indicated.only_if: plain films and ultrasound are nondiagnostic and the infant is stable

not_indicated.why: Does not diagnose necrotizing enterocolitis and risks aspiration; used only to evaluate malrotation when suspected
Urinary tract infection does not mimic necrotizing enterocolitis in this population
Pancreatitis is not part of the differential in a premature newborn with abdominal distension
No role in the evaluation of neonatal bowel ischemia

decision_points: Stop all enteral feeds and start nasogastric decompression as soon as the diagnosis is suspected
Obtain supine and left lateral decubitus abdominal films; free intraperitoneal air means immediate surgical consultation
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics after blood cultures; do not delay for imaging
A rapidly falling platelet count, rising lactate or fixed dilated loop suggests perforation and need for surgery
Distinguish from Clostridioides difficile colitis, which typically follows antibiotic exposure and presents with profuse watery diarrhea rather than pneumatosis

criteria.name: Modified Bell staging
criteria.summary: Clinical staging system that grades necrotizing enterocolitis from suspected disease (stage I: feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, temperature instability) through definite disease (stage II: pneumatosis on x-ray, with or without portal venous gas) to advanced disease (stage III: deteriorating vital signs, peritonitis, acidosis, thrombocytopenia, and either ascites or pneumoperitoneum).
items: Stage I: nonspecific systemic and abdominal signs, normal or nonspecific x-ray
Stage II: pneumatosis intestinalis on x-ray, with or without portal venous gas
Stage III: systemic deterioration, peritonitis, acidosis, thrombocytopenia, ascites or pneumoperitoneum

differential.name: Clostridioides difficile colitis
differential.why_considered: Both cause abdominal distension, bloody stools and systemic toxicity in a hospitalized infant, and both can follow antibiotic exposure.
differential.trigger: Profuse watery diarrhea after antibiotics, with marked abdominal distension and systemic toxicity

history: Recent or ongoing antibiotic exposure
Profuse watery diarrhea, often without gross blood early
Usually older infants or children rather than extremely premature newborns
exam: Abdominal distension with tenderness, sometimes with signs of toxic megacolon
Systemic toxicity out of proportion to abdominal findings early
labs: Positive stool C. difficile toxin or PCR
imaging: Colonic dilation with thumbprinting or toxic megacolon
No pneumatosis intestinalis or portal venous gas

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: Premature infants with sepsis present with lethargy, temperature instability, apnea, bradycardia and feeding intolerance, closely mimicking early necrotizing enterocolitis.
differential.trigger: Temperature instability, apnea and lethargy in a premature infant with a soft, nondistended abdomen

history: Risk factors for sepsis such as prolonged rupture of membranes or maternal fever
Symptoms may precede any abdominal findings
No bloody stools early
exam: No abdominal wall erythema or rigidity
labs: Leukocytosis or leukopenia with left shift
Lactate may be elevated but pneumatosis is absent
imaging: Abdominal x-ray shows normal or nonspecific bowel gas without pneumatosis or portal venous gas

differential.name: Malrotation with midgut volvulus
differential.why_considered: Bilious vomiting and abdominal distension in a neonate can suggest necrotizing enterocolitis, but volvulus is a surgical emergency with a different mechanism.
differential.trigger: Bilious vomiting in a well-appearing infant with a scaphoid abdomen

history: Bilious vomiting, often sudden and recurrent
Infant may appear well between episodes early
No bloody stools initially
exam: Abdomen may be scaphoid or mildly distended
Signs of shock if bowel is infarcted
imaging: Upper gastrointestinal series shows abnormal duodenojejunal junction or corkscrew sign
Abdominal x-ray may show double-bubble or paucity of gas

differential.name: Hirschsprung disease with enterocolitis
differential.why_considered: Can present with abdominal distension, vomiting and bloody diarrhea in a neonate, and enterocolitis is a serious complication.

history: Failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours
Chronic constipation before the acute illness
Often term infant
exam: Abdominal distension with a tight anal sphincter on rectal exam
Explosive release of stool and gas after rectal examination
labs: No specific laboratory finding; may have leukocytosis
Stool may be positive for blood
imaging: Barium enema shows a transition zone with a narrow aganglionic segment

differential.name: Pyloric stenosis
differential.why_considered: Non-bilious projectile vomiting in a young infant can be confused with feeding intolerance of necrotizing enterocolitis.

history: Projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds
Infant is hungry and thriving between feeds
Usually 3–6 weeks old, often term
exam: Palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant
imaging: Ultrasound shows thickened and elongated pylorus
Abdominal x-ray shows a dilated stomach with paucity of distal gas

differential.name: Neonatal bowel obstruction (atresia or meconium ileus)
differential.why_considered: Presents with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension and failure to pass meconium, overlapping with necrotizing enterocolitis.

history: Failure to pass meconium in the first day
Bilious vomiting from birth
May have polyhydramnios history
exam: No abdominal wall erythema or systemic toxicity early
labs: May have electrolyte abnormalities but no thrombocytopenia or severe acidosis
imaging: Abdominal x-ray shows dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels and a paucity of distal gas
Contrast enema may show a microcolon

differential.name: Spontaneous intestinal perforation
differential.why_considered: Very low birth weight infants can present with sudden abdominal distension and pneumoperitoneum, mimicking perforated necrotizing enterocolitis.

history: Sudden onset in the first week of life, often before feeds are advanced
Often associated with indomethacin or steroid exposure
exam: Abdominal distension with discoloration but often less diffuse tenderness
labs: Metabolic acidosis and thrombocytopenia may be present
imaging: Abdominal x-ray shows free air but no intramural gas

severity.mild: Suspected disease (Bell stage I): feeding intolerance with large gastric residuals, mild abdominal distension, temperature instability, and nonspecific or normal abdominal x-ray.
severity.moderate: Definite disease (Bell stage II): pneumatosis intestinalis on x-ray with or without portal venous gas, abdominal tenderness, metabolic acidosis, and thrombocytopenia.
severity.severe: Advanced disease (Bell stage III): deteriorating vital signs, peritonitis, severe acidosis, marked thrombocytopenia, ascites or pneumoperitoneum, often requiring surgery.
severity.critical: Perforation with diffuse peritonitis and septic shock: rigid abdomen, hypotension, apnea, bradycardia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and multi-organ failure.

red_flags.meaning: Bowel perforation; requires immediate surgical consultation

red_flags.finding: Rigid abdomen or abdominal wall erythema
red_flags.meaning: Peritonitis or bowel necrosis; surgical emergency
Progressive disease and risk of perforation; reassess urgently

red_flags.finding: Rising lactate or worsening metabolic acidosis
red_flags.meaning: Intestinal ischemia and systemic hypoperfusion; consider surgery
Septic shock; aggressive resuscitation and surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Fixed, dilated loop of bowel on serial films
red_flags.meaning: Nonviable bowel; surgical intervention likely needed

complications.name: Intestinal stricture
clues: Recurrent abdominal distension and vomiting weeks after recovery

special_populations.differences: The youngest and smallest premature infants may show only apnea, bradycardia, temperature instability and poor feeding before abdominal signs appear; a high index of suspicion is needed.
Term infants account for a minority of cases and often have a predisposing condition such as congenital heart disease, sepsis or a hypoxic-ischemic event; abdominal signs may be the first clue.

Infants with severe immunodeficiency or on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics can present with a picture overlapping Clostridioides difficile colitis, with profuse diarrhea and marked systemic toxicity.

key_questions.question: How premature was your baby, and how much did he weigh at birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Birth before 32 weeks and weight under 1500 g; the strongest risk factors

key_questions.question: How old is your baby now, and how many days has he been in the nursery?
key_questions.looking_for: First 2–4 weeks of life, typically 1–3 weeks after birth

key_questions.question: When did the belly start looking swollen, and has it gotten worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over hours to a day or two, with progressive distension

key_questions.question: Has he been tolerating his feeds, or are there large residuals left in his stomach?
key_questions.looking_for: Feeding intolerance with large gastric residuals, the earliest sign

key_questions.question: Has he vomited, and was it green or bloody?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilious or bloody emesis suggests advanced disease

key_questions.question: Have you seen blood in his diaper or bloody mucus in the stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Gross blood in the stool, present in about half of cases

key_questions.question: Has he had any spells where he stops breathing or his heart rate drops?
key_questions.looking_for: Apnea and bradycardia spells, a sign of systemic illness

key_questions.question: Has his temperature been unstable, either low or high?
key_questions.looking_for: Temperature instability, common in the sick premature infant

key_questions.question: Is he more sleepy or less responsive than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Lethargy and decreased responsiveness suggesting systemic illness

key_questions.question: Is he breast-milk-fed or formula-fed?
key_questions.looking_for: Formula feeding carries higher risk than human milk

key_questions.question: Has he had any antibiotics, umbilical lines, or indomethacin or ibuprofen?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotics, umbilical artery catheterization, or cyclooxygenase inhibitors for a patent ductus arteriosus

key_questions.question: Did he have any trouble around birth, such as a low oxygen level or resuscitation?
Does he have any heart condition or other birth defects?
key_questions.looking_for: Congenital heart disease with ductal-dependent circulation, especially in term infants

key_questions.question: Has he had profuse watery diarrhea, especially after antibiotics?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests Clostridioides difficile colitis rather than necrotizing enterocolitis

key_questions.question: Did he pass meconium in the first 48 hours after birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Delayed meconium suggests Hirschsprung disease or obstruction

reasoning_points: Premature, very low birth weight infant in the first weeks of life with feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and bloody stools
Abdominal distension and tenderness with large gastric residuals are the earliest and most consistent findings
Bilious emesis, apnea, bradycardia, temperature instability and lethargy indicate systemic illness
Risk factors include prematurity, very low birth weight, formula feeding, perinatal asphyxia and umbilical artery catheterization
Abdominal x-ray showing pneumatosis intestinalis, with or without portal venous gas, confirms the diagnosis
Thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis, hyponatremia and elevated lactate track severity and risk of perforation
Pneumoperitoneum or a fixed dilated loop on serial films means perforation and requires immediate surgical consultation
Distinguish from Clostridioides difficile colitis, neonatal sepsis, malrotation with volvulus, Hirschsprung disease, pyloric stenosis and spontaneous intestinal perforation

easy: Premature infant of very low birth weight in the second or third week of life
Feeding intolerance with large residuals and progressive abdominal distension
medium: Early disease with only feeding intolerance and mild distension and a nonspecific abdominal film
Term infant with a predisposing condition such as congenital heart disease or a hypoxic event
Overlap with neonatal sepsis where abdominal signs are subtle
Thrombocytopenia and metabolic acidosis without overt pneumatosis
hard: Extremely premature infant presenting only with apnea, bradycardia and temperature instability before any abdominal signs
Infant with a picture overlapping Clostridioides difficile colitis after prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics
Sudden deterioration from perforation with pneumoperitoneum but no prior pneumatosis
Distinguishing from spontaneous intestinal perforation in the first week of life
Bilious vomiting in a well-appearing infant with a scaphoid abdomen suggesting malrotation with volvulus instead
